tooltip.title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA)
tooltip.markdown: A rare, chronic autoimmune disease caused by antibodies to Type VII collagen. Presents with skin fragility and blistering.

tooltip.title: Pathophysiology of EBA
tooltip.markdown: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita

tooltip.title: Target Antigen
tooltip.markdown: Autoantibodies (IgG) against Type VII Collagen, the main component of anchoring fibrils

tooltip.title: Mechanism
tooltip.markdown: Disruption of anchoring fibrils weakens dermo-epidermal adhesion

tooltip.title: Blister Level
tooltip.markdown: Subepidermal split deep in the sub-lamina densa

tooltip.title: Classical Form
tooltip.markdown: Resembles hereditary dystrophic EB. Skin fragility, trauma-induced tense bullae, atrophic scarring, and milia formation

tooltip.title: Inflammatory Form
tooltip.markdown: Can mimic Bullous Pemphigoid, with widespread tense bullae on inflamed skin and intense pruritus

tooltip.title: Direct Immunofluorescence
tooltip.markdown: Linear IgG and C3 deposition at the BMZ

tooltip.title: Salt-Split Skin
tooltip.markdown: The key diagnostic test. Shows antibody binding to the dermal side (floor) of the split

tooltip.title: Serology
tooltip.markdown: ELISA for anti-Type VII Collagen antibodies is available

tooltip.title: Treatment of EBA
tooltip.markdown: Therapeutic approaches for epidermolysis bullosa acquisita

tooltip.title: First Line Treatment
tooltip.markdown: Often difficult to treat. Colchicine or Dapsone can be effective, especially for the inflammatory variant

tooltip.title: Refractory Disease Treatment
tooltip.markdown: Systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, IVIG, and Rituximab
